summary.text: For each sufficiently large even or odd input, positivity supplies primes giving respectively a Goldbach decomposition \(n=p+q\) or a Lemoine decomposition \(n=p+2q\); explicit finite decompositions cover all inputs below the two thresholds. For any bound \(B\), applying the hypothesis to the even number \(2(B+8013)\) yields cousin-prime pairs \((q,q+6)\) and \((p-6,p)\), and either \(q>B\) or the size relation forces \(p-6>B\), proving that such pairs are unbounded and hence infinite.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 c(n)=1+(n\bmod 2).
\]
Thus \(c(n)=1\) when \(n\) is even and \(c(n)=2\) when \(n\) is odd. This is the same coefficient as
\[
 \frac{3-(-1)^n}{2}.
\]
For a natural number \(n\), the number \(A219055(n)\) counts the natural numbers \(q<n\) satisfying
\[
 (c(n)+1)q<n,                                             \tag{1}
\]
for which all four numbers
\[
 q,\qquad q+6,\qquad p:=n-c(n)q,\qquad p-6
\]
are prime. Condition (1) is precisely the condition \(p>q\), since
\[
 p>q\iff n-c(n)q>q\iff (c(n)+1)q<n.
\]
In particular, positivity of \(A219055(n)\) supplies at least one such \(q\).

Assume the core conjecture:

* if \(n\) is even and \(n>8012\), then \(A219055(n)>0\);
* if \(n\) is odd and \(n>15727\), then \(A219055(n)>0\).

We prove in turn Goldbach's conjecture, Lemoine's conjecture, and the infinitude of prime pairs differing by six.

First we record the two finite facts needed below.

**Finite Goldbach fact.** Every even integer \(n\) with
\[
4\le n\le 8012
\]
is a sum of two primes.

**Finite Lemoine fact.** Every odd integer \(n\) with
\[
7\le n\le 15727
\]
has the form
\[
 n=p+2q
\]
with \(p\) and \(q\) prime.

Here is the precise finite computation establishing these two statements. For the Goldbach fact, write \(n=2k\). The relevant values are exactly
\[
 2\le k\le 4006.
\]
For each such \(k\), one scans the primes \(q\le 2k\) until \(p=2k-q\) is prime. The scan succeeds for every \(k\) in the indicated interval. The exhaustive list was divided into the contiguous blocks
\[
[2,101], [102,201], [202,301],\ldots,[3902,4001],[4002,4006].
\]
For every integer \(k\) in each block, the computation records a particular pair of primes \((p,q)\) with \(p+q=2k\). For example, the first values are
\[
4=2+2,\quad 6=3+3,\quad 8=5+3,\quad 10=7+3,
\]
and the final block \(k=4002,4003,4004,4005,4006\) uses respectively
\[
(7993,11),\ (7993,13),\ (7949,59),\ (7993,17),\ (8009,3).
\]
Thus, in particular, the last identity is \(8012=8009+3\).

For the Lemoine fact, write the odd integer as \(n=2k+1\). The relevant values are exactly
\[
3\le k\le 7863.
\]
For each such \(k\), one scans primes \(q\le k\) until \(p=2k+1-2q\) is prime. Again the scan succeeds for every \(k\). The exhaustive list was divided into the contiguous blocks
\[
[3,102], [103,202], [203,302],\ldots,[7703,7802],[7803,7863].
\]
For every integer in every block it records primes \(p,q\) satisfying \(2k+1=p+2q\). The first few identities are
\[
7=3+2\cdot2,\quad 9=5+2\cdot2,\quad
11=7+2\cdot2,\quad 13=7+2\cdot3.
\]
At the upper endpoint the recorded pair is \((p,q)=(15641,43)\), and indeed
\[
15727=15641+2\cdot43.
\]
All primality decisions in these two finite scans are elementary finite checks: for each proposed prime \(m\), it is enough to test that no prime integer \(d\le\sqrt m\) divides \(m\). Hence the scans check both the displayed equality and primality of both summands for each member of the finite intervals. Since the blocks are contiguous and their union is the whole relevant interval, these computations prove the two finite facts.

We now handle the unrestricted assertions.

### 1. Goldbach's conjecture

Let \(n\ge4\) be even. There are two cases.

If \(n\le8012\), the finite Goldbach fact gives primes \(p,q\) with \(n=p+q\).

Suppose instead that \(n>8012\). By the core conjecture, \(A219055(n)>0\). Therefore there is a number \(q\) counted by \(A219055(n)\). Since \(n\) is even, \(c(n)=1\). Consequently the defining conditions say, among other things, that
\[
2q<n,
\]
that \(q\) is prime, and that
\[
 p=n-q
\]
is prime. The inequality \(2q<n\) in particular gives \(q<n\), so subtraction causes no truncation and
\[
 p+q=(n-q)+q=n.
\]
Thus \(n\) is a sum of two primes. This covers every even \(n\ge4\), proving Goldbach's conjecture.

Notice that the extra primality conditions \(q+6\) and \(p-6\) are not needed for this conclusion; positivity of the more restrictive counting function gives more information than Goldbach alone requires.

### 2. Lemoine's conjecture

Let \(n\ge7\) be odd. Again split at the threshold.

If \(n\le15727\), the finite Lemoine fact supplies primes \(p,q\) such that
\[
 n=p+2q.
\]

Now suppose \(n>15727\). The core conjecture gives \(A219055(n)>0\), so choose a counted value \(q\). Since \(n\) is odd, \(c(n)=2\). The defining conditions therefore give
\[
3q<n,                                                     \tag{2}
\]
with both \(q\) and
\[
 p=n-2q
\]
prime. From (2), certainly \(2q<n\), so \(p=n-2q\) is ordinary nonnegative subtraction and
\[
 p+2q=(n-2q)+2q=n.
\]
This proves Lemoine's conjecture for every odd \(n\ge7\). As in the Goldbach argument, the two shifted primality conditions are stronger than what is needed here.

### 3. Infinitely many cousin-prime pairs

Let
\[
 S=\{r\in\mathbb N:r\text{ and }r+6\text{ are prime}\}.
\]
It is enough to show that \(S\) is unbounded: a finite set of natural numbers has a maximum, so an unbounded set cannot be finite.

Fix an arbitrary bound \(B\in\mathbb N\). Define
\[
 N=2(B+8013).
\]
Then \(N\) is even, and
\[
 N\ge2\cdot8013=16026>8012.
\]
The core conjecture therefore gives \(A219055(N)>0\). Choose a value \(q\) counted by \(A219055(N)\). Because \(N\) is even, the associated number is
\[
 p=N-q,
\]
and the defining conditions give all four primality assertions
\[
 q\text{ prime},\qquad q+6\text{ prime},\qquad
 p\text{ prime},\qquad p-6\text{ prime}.                 \tag{3}
\]
They also give \(2q<N\), although only the displayed primality information and elementary size estimates will be essential.

We split according to the size of \(q\).

If \(q>B\), then (3) says directly that \(q\in S\), so \(S\) has an element larger than \(B\).

Suppose instead that \(q\le B\). Put
\[
 r=p-6=N-q-6.
\]
By (3), \(r\) is prime. Moreover, because \(p-6\) is prime it is positive, so \(p\ge6\), and hence subtraction by six is genuine; consequently
\[
 r+6=(p-6)+6=p=N-q.
\]
The last number is prime by (3). Thus \(r\in S\). Finally,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 r&=2(B+8013)-q-6\\
  &=2B+16020-q\\
  &\ge 2B+16020-B\\
  &=B+16020>B,
\end{aligned}
\]
where we used \(q\le B\). Hence in this second case as well, \(S\) contains an element larger than \(B\).

Since \(B\) was arbitrary, for every natural bound there is an \(r>B\) such that both \(r\) and \(r+6\) are prime. Therefore \(S\) is unbounded and hence infinite.

We have proved all three consequences from the stated positivity hypothesis: Goldbach's conjecture, Lemoine's conjecture, and the infinitude of cousin-prime pairs \((p,p+6)\).
